# Isolated publication writer

Read your complete execution plan and its entire lossless reader, including every shared block, in bounded untruncated outputs. Only the plan and reader are allowed evidence. Do not inspect peers, sessions, credentials, other debates or environment; do not browse, make paid calls or spawn agents. Report complete reading and the sole absolute output, then wait for controller authenticated reading release before authoring. Use the frozen source, resolved judgments, calculated scores and skeleton. Preserve identity, motion, scope, section/card order, times, numbers and assessment substance. Reference profiles provide a comparison corpus, never debate evidence or reusable prose.

Output exactly {summary,quotes,moves,overall,logicalExtension,noveltyMap,editorialReview}. Do not output another assembled candidate. The checker inserts these leaves into the immutable skeleton.

- summary: 8–35 words describing the assessed exchange and its result fairly.
- quotes: {pro:{text,context},con:{text,context}}. Text is a verbatim frozen quoteEligibleExactSpans string of that side, 3–18 words; preserve source case and punctuation. Read each without its context: it must express a complete thought, retaining any meaning-changing qualification. Contexts are 12–55 words; they explain use, not complete a fragment. Prefer clearly articulated claims over pronoun-dependent snippets or biographical remarks.
- moves: exactly 32 entries in skeleton publication order (section, exchange, pro then con), each {moveId,words,critique}. Description normally 22–28 words: actual claim, support/comparison and implication, without padding or invented premises. Mean at least20.9; no more than25% below20words. No tags yet.
- Each critique has exactly four sentences, beginning Strongest feature:, Principal limitation:, Live burden:, Locked score:, in that order. 105–130 words AND at least880 characters; target112–122 substantive words while satisfying both gates. The last sentence states the exact card score as N/100 with a specific explanation. Every sentence ends with terminal punctuation; avoid internal full stops in abbreviations. Discuss the actual inference, evidence, limitation and remaining burden. Do not turn withholding assent into an obligation to prove the contrary. Write source-specific prose manually, without interchangeable sentence-bank bodies, padded suffixes or repeated templates. Common six-word sequences present in at least one-quarter of critiques may cover at most15% of words on average and25% in any critique.
- overall: {pro:{strengths:[...],blunders:[{text,links:[]},...]},con:...}. At least3 concrete strengths and2 material blunders each, normally18–35words per item. Remain score-consistent; no invented claims, new numerical penalties or speculative labels. Links remain empty until separate rhetorical review.
- logicalExtension: {pro:{finalArgument:{thesis,premises,conclusion},newArguments:[{title,text},...]},con:...}. Thesis at least12words; four to six premises each at least12words; conclusion at least15words. Two to four distinct reinforcing arguments per side, title2–8words, text45–130words, preferably80–110 substantive words. The whole section is visibly labeled AI Contribution. Within it write direct philosophical prose, without repeated provenance or generic model/constraint framing. Strengthen both sides proportionately, distinguish new reasoning from recorded contributions, and preserve the question and opponent burden. Each reinforcing argument needs a genuinely new inference beyond the inventory. Preserve natural punctuation. Compare both sides' openings, sentence structures and conclusions for mirrored scaffolds and noun-swappable prose; compare the supplied independent corpus without recycling it.
- noveltyMap: one {side,title,closestMoveIds:[...],distinctInferentialContribution} for every reinforcing argument. Identify a concrete inferential addition, not a generic novelty assertion.
- editorialReview: {sourceFidelity,completeQuotes,scoreConsistency,nonformulaicCritiques,aiContributionNonformulaic,aiPunctuation,referenceComparison}. Each is a source-specific string at least40characters describing a review actually performed.

## Frozen source constraints

# Frozen source restrictions — debate 307

Question: Does the Bible misquote Jesus?
Pro: Bart Ehrman. Con: James White. Event: January 21, 2009, Fort Lauderdale. The publisher’s event listing establishes identity and date only; outside commentary and later scholarship are not assessment evidence.

The controller read all 4,152 canonical events, including both closings and excluded audience material. The indexed transcript uses ZERO-BASED event numbers before each timestamp. All startEvent/endEvent fields use these same zero-based indices. Canonical captions remain unchanged.

## Scope and attribution

Assess the two formal openings, both rebuttals, both cross-examinations and both closing statements, approximately 0:23–2:28:59. Retain events 9–3757; exclude the copyright preamble and all audience Q&A/outro beginning with event 3758. The word “prohibited” at the start of event 9 belongs to the preceding copyright announcement. Event 3758 joins White’s final “hearing” with the first audience question; neither fragment is needed as assessment evidence. Brief timekeeping, thanks, laughter and conversational logistics provide no substantive argument. No credit, penalty, inferred concession or alleged failure to reply may rely on excluded material. The complete transcript is provided for scope auditing, not permission to score Q&A.

Opening ownership: Ehrman from event 9 through 765; White begins “good evening” within 766 and ends within 1539. Ehrman begins “okay thank you” within 1539 and ends “yes” within 1892. White begins “it is a little bit difficult” within 1892 and continues through 2276. Ehrman leads questioning from 2277 through 2779; White leads from 2780 through 3271’s initial carryover. Ehrman’s closing starts “one of my tasks” within 3271 and ends within 3505. White’s closing starts “well first of all” within 3505 and ends at 3757, with the last word carried into excluded 3758. Do not assign preceding-speaker carryover to the next speaker. Cross-examination answers belong to the named respondent, not the questioner. Retain the immediate question when needed to interpret an answer. A selected mixed span must explicitly identify the scored words and exclude the opponent’s interjection from its claim or quote.

Exactly two substantive advocates carry the motion. The recording has formal rounds, so no team or moderator-advocacy exception is used. The anonymous timekeeper’s interjections are logistical. Any remaining uncertainty that is material to a selected claim must trigger below-high attribution and required audio verification; do not hide it behind a blanket caption caveat.

## Burdens and qualifications

1. Preserve the stated question byte-for-byte. Both speakers accept textual variation. Ehrman argues that surviving copies sometimes change important wording and that recovering an early common ancestor does not guarantee every original word. White defends reliable preservation/recoverability through the collective manuscript tradition and continuity of the apostolic message. Do not turn White into an advocate of perfect individual copies or Ehrman into an advocate that nothing historical can be known. Do not silently substitute “Is Christianity false?” or “Is every part of the New Testament unreliable?”

2. Distinguish three claims: a local textual difference, a significant interpretive difference, and loss of the overall message. Agreement on the first does not settle the other two. White calls variants important and worthy of study while disputing their effect on the message. Ehrman expressly concedes that the vast majority of variants are insignificant or untranslatable spelling differences, around 18:59–20:13. Do not use the raw variant count as though he argued that all variants substantially alter meaning.

3. Ehrman’s opening presents lost originals, delayed surviving witnesses and copying errors; early circulation examples are illustrative reconstructions. White counters that a larger manuscript population produces a larger variant count and that early geographically dispersed witnesses help reconstruction. Treat dates, quantities and manuscript relationships as claims supported or challenged in this debate, not facts independently established by this assessment.

4. White explicitly compares representative PRINTED editions, not individual manuscripts, at 43:19 and in rebuttal. His roughly 95% claim uses all words; percentages assigning manuscripts to families use variant units. Ehrman separately challenges extrapolation from printed editions to actual manuscript word agreement. Preserve both denominator and evidence-type distinctions. White’s admission he has not collated a Byzantine manuscript is not itself a refutation of a reproducible printed-edition calculation. Ehrman’s “200 within 300 years” is a misstatement immediately corrected to White’s 120 and acknowledged; do not score the mistaken 200 as White’s claim.

5. The captions corrupt “four-tenths” at about 40:30 as “410” and contain numerous personal-name, Greek-word, manuscript-date and reference errors. The supporting audio check clarifies four-tenths; no rating or quotation may depend on the recognition error. White’s dozen manuscripts within a century is challenged on dating; he cites Wallace, Comfort and Skeat and gives examples but does not supply a full list in that exchange. Do not invent the list or independently resolve the dating from outside scholarship.

6. White’s tenacity claim is that the original reading survives among the alternatives in the collective tradition, not that any single manuscript or modern edition is infallible. Multiple streams and intersecting transmission are offered against a simple linear telephone-game model. His P75/Vaticanus argument distinguishes independent copies from a direct parent–child relationship. Not being direct copies does not by itself establish separate access to the autograph. Ehrman’s later hypothetical bottleneck accepts subsequent multiple lines while questioning what happened before the branching.

7. Both appeal to scholarly authorities. Their lists of living scholars, consensus claims and reported book passages are claims presented here. Do not resolve the debate by credentials or import external consensus. Ehrman acknowledges he does not know Barbara Aland’s view when asked. White cites scholarship and his own study, and characterizes some contrary trends as postmodern; assess any relevant inference rather than the label alone.

8. At approximately 1:49:52 onward, White tests whether P52 variation changes the entire meaning. Ehrman distinguishes a significant difference from a complete meaning reversal and discusses reconstruction in a lacuna. Greek phonetics and missing-word reconstructions are recognition-sensitive: do not make an exact Greek reading load-bearing without verified text. Ehrman does NOT say surviving originals are logically impossible. He distinguishes possibility from probability and offers the conjectural Enoch reading of 1 Peter 3:19 as an example, not a demonstrated lost original.

9. Ehrman’s response to percentages uses the example of one negation changing a hundred-word passage. This concerns semantic impact, not a claim that every small variation has such an effect. In the Hebrews “apart from God/by the grace of God” exchange, distinguish whether a specific passage explicitly teaches abandonment from whether that theme is consistent with the rest of Hebrews. The two standards must not be collapsed.

10. Ehrman accepts the same uncertainty about original wording for classical literature, while still using surviving witnesses for historical work. He does not accept that uncertainty about some words destroys all historical knowledge. White’s classical comparison concerns relative attestation and consistency of standards. His broader skeptical-consequence inference must be evaluated against Ehrman’s actual limited uncertainty, not against an invented total skepticism.

11. At about 1:59:23, Ehrman agrees his hypothetical edited Greek text would differ less from a standard critical text than the Textus Receptus does. He later declines an unexamined translation comparison and maintains that significance is not measured by word percentage. Do not treat the limited Greek-edition concession as surrender of all his claims about interpretive differences.

12. For Mark 1:41, White challenges the single free-writing witness and suggests contextual harmonization as an explanation for anger. Ehrman grounds his preference in internal reasoning about a harder reading being softened, not in a general endorsement of Bezae’s reliability. Around 2:03:16 he explicitly describes the effect as a fuller picture or different nuance, not an entirely different book. This qualification governs broader summaries of the example.

13. At about 2:04:43–2:05:47, Ehrman’s Philippians third-copy scenario is a hypothetical countermodel: later agreement can identify a common ancestor without proving that ancestor exactly reproduces the autograph. It is not documented knowledge that all Philippians manuscripts actually descend from an erroneous third copy. His closing explicitly accepts multiple subsequent lines. White appeals to early dispersed transmission and asks what positive evidence establishes primitive corruption. Distinguish a counterexample to a guarantee from proof of actual corruption.

14. Inspiration is related but not identical to the textual motion. Ehrman labels his expectation about preservation personal and says it motivated his interest, while also defending it in replies and his closing. He allows possible divine inspiration without perfect preservation and concedes the apostles did not share his own standard. White argues that inspiration need not entail perfect individual copies and that apostolic use of variant translations rebuts that requirement. Neither speaker’s religious identity substitutes for this argument.

15. The closing material matters. Ehrman emphasizes meaningful readings, the gap between earliest recoverable and original text, and Bibles as historically available manuscripts. White distinguishes textual variants from misquotation, argues continuity of theology, quotes Ehrman’s agreement about essential beliefs and urges Christian education. The quoted agreement is White’s presented quotation, not a new live concession. White’s comments about public misuse of Ehrman concern third parties; do not attribute those third-party claims to Ehrman, who explicitly disclaims control of others’ uses. Do not penalize Ehrman for not answering White’s last closing.

16. Q&A material after 2:28:59 is excluded: the Pauline collection claim, eyewitness/community safeguards introduced in that answer, Dead Sea Scroll comparisons, audience questions about personal opinions, historical Jesus probabilities, later John 8 authenticity discussion, necktie gift and final inerrancy answer. Earlier independent arguments on related topics remain eligible only on their retained evidence. No answer in Q&A can rescue or undermine an assessed formal-round move.

17. Five targeted automated audio-to-text checks supplement complete public-caption reading. These are neither direct human listening nor speaker diarization. The primary caption stream, including harmless recognition errors, remains the canonical exact-quote source. Do not silently fix an exact quotation. Audio checks support wording review only where their clips actually cover the source.

18. Featured quotes must be exact 3–18 word complete standalone thoughts with clear referents and necessary qualifications. Avoid Greek fragments, ambiguous “this/that” fragments and concessions severed from their immediate limitation. If a complete and fair thought cannot fit, choose another passage. No invented completion words. Both sides must have at least one eligible candidate before inventory freezes.


## Exact candidate transport

After authenticated reading release, construct the complete candidate in memory. Preserve it with functions.exec store/load. Run the pinned checker through noninteractive stdin with tty:false and safe shell quoting, never a disk draft or interactive PTY. Ordinary unsaved mechanical corrections remain in this same context. Emit the exact checked raw UTF-8 JSON string using the transport key assigned by the controller in a sufficiently large tool response, plus its SHA-256 and byte count. The controller transports those same emitted bytes into the maintained memory handoff, reads every field and alone releases its first save. Do not start a socket, create candidate files, overwrite outputs or perform post-save authoring. One fresh context, one saved submission, zero automatic retries. Reading must be tool-visible in separate bounded responses, including every shared block; never redirect reader output to a file or /dev/null, and never claim a hash as proof of reading.

## Card-specific evidence discipline

Write each card from that move's frozen claim, warrant, source and resolved dimensions. Adjacent moves may clarify a reply but cannot silently replace the selected argument. In particular, the count-context move concerns abundance producing both variants and comparative evidence; the next taxonomy move separately introduces meaningful and viable categories. The initial Mark anger example contrasts emotions; the later internal-evidence move separately argues a harder reading was softened. The corrected Suetonius follow-up concerns continued scholarly quotation, not the subsequent hypothetical Greek-edition comparison.

Derive every stated defect from the final ledger rather than inventing a sharper criticism for rhetorical balance. A challenge to a guarantee need not establish that the contrary event probably occurred. A limited or qualified claim must not become total skepticism, proof of actual early corruption, perfect individual-copy preservation, or an allegation that all textual variants change doctrine. Keep the limited Greek-edition agreement, the printed-word denominator, the later Mark nuance, and the published essential-beliefs quotation's qualification distinct. Describing a different standard does not by itself establish equivocation. Each fourth critique sentence must give both the exact score and a concrete reason for that score; a bare score with its explanation attached to another label is insufficient.

For new reinforcing arguments, name the nearest recorded reasoning and explain the added inference before acceptance. Renaming distributed transmission, doctrinal redundancy, the shared-ancestor limitation, or the distinction between local wording and the whole message is not a new argument. Use direct philosophical prose with distinct reasoning on each side.

value.title: Bart Ehrman vs James White — Does the Bible Misquote Jesus? (2009)
value.label: Does the Bible Misquote Jesus?
value.sourceNote: This assessment covers both formal openings, rebuttals, cross-examinations and closing statements, approximately 0:23–2:28:59. Audience Q&A, logistical interjections and the outro are excluded and supply no credit, penalty or inference of a failure to reply. Both speakers accept textual variants: Ehrman argues that important wording changed and some originals remain uncertain; White defends reliable recovery and continuity of the New Testament’s message. Each is assessed on the position actually defended. Public automatic captions were supplemented by five targeted automated audio checks; these were not direct human listening. The complete public caption record was retained for scope and attribution checks. Exact quotations preserve caption wording; argument summaries and critiques are condensed assessments, and manuscript dates, counts and scholarly claims are evaluated as presented in the debate. One long automated audio check ended before its clip ended; no independent audio verification is claimed beyond the text actually returned.
value.scoringNote: Scores are AI-generated estimates of argumentative performance, rather than judgments about worldview truth; the separate AI Contribution does not affect these scores.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Successive hand copies inherited and added mistakes while originals disappeared.
moves.warrant: Ehrman joins inherited errors, new errors, and loss of correcting exemplars.
moves.inference: Survivors cannot simply be assumed to preserve every original word.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 144–209 begin when Ehrman states that the first copy made mistakes and end after he completes the sequence of inherited errors, attempted corrections, and loss of the original and early copies.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 144–283 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The copying mechanism matters because inherited errors plus lost exemplars explain why a large surviving tradition can still depart from the originals.

burdenContact.rationale: The pro recovery route depends on whether the copying process could sever surviving wording from the lost originals; this move supplies that mechanism.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The woman-taken-in-adultery story was inserted by scribes rather than originally written in John.
moves.warrant: Ehrman says the passage is absent from the oldest authorities despite its popularity.
moves.inference: A famous Jesus story can appear in Bibles without being original New Testament text.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 591–651 begin with Ehrman’s insertion claim and end after his manuscript-based conclusion; the intervening narrative is needed to identify the exact story whose textual status he disputes.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 591–651 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The adultery story is a concrete, familiar passage that entered later copies, showing that a beloved unit can be absent from the earliest recoverable text.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro misquotation status by identifying a whole passage printed as scripture although it was not in the earliest recoverable Gospel text.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The final twelve verses of Mark were added after the Gospel originally ended at 16:8.
moves.warrant: Ehrman contrasts the abrupt ending with the later resurrection appearances and signs absent from the oldest witnesses.
moves.inference: A substantial block about Jesus can be transmitted as Scripture although it was not original to Mark.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 652–715 contain the original-ending claim, the content supplied by the added ending, and the conclusion about the oldest witnesses; all three identify the load-bearing example.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 652–715 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Mark’s longer ending supplies resurrection appearances and signs, so its later addition bears directly on whether every printed Gospel passage preserves Mark’s wording.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro misquotation status because the familiar ending attributes material to Mark that the earliest evidence does not.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: The prayer from the cross and the end-times saying contain disputed words attributed directly to Jesus.
moves.warrant: Ehrman notes omissions in early manuscripts for Luke 23:34 and Matthew 24.
moves.inference: At some sayings, which words Jesus is represented as speaking depends on the manuscript.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 717–765 contain two short saying examples and Ehrman’s concluding uncertainty claim; the pair supports the motion without repeating the longer added-passage cases.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 717–765 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The disputed sayings turn the textual question into a historical one: some words printed as Jesus’ speech may not have been written by the evangelists.

burdenContact.rationale: This reaches the motion’s attribution bridge by arguing that later textual additions can be presented as words of Jesus.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: More manuscripts produce more variants while providing more reconstructive evidence.
moves.warrant: White links abundance to both the count and confidence from early varied witnesses.
moves.inference: The headline total is misleading without historical context.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 868–926 begin with White’s summary of the raw-variant argument and end after his completed inference that manuscript abundance can increase both variants and reconstructive evidence; later taxonomy is separately inventoried.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 868–940 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: White’s count comparison is needed to test whether the headline number of variants is meaningful without relating it to the size and repetition of the manuscript tradition.

burdenContact.rationale: This bears on the con significance route because a raw variant total is probative only after accounting for the unusually large corpus being compared.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Only a limited subset of variants is both meaningful and viable, and many differences have ordinary scribal explanations.
moves.warrant: White distinguishes non-meaningful, nonviable, accidental, harmonized, and purposeful changes before estimating the relevant subset.
moves.inference: The existence of variants does not make every variant a plausible alternative affecting interpretation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 955–1027 supply White’s complete classification and the estimate that depends on it; stopping earlier would omit viability, while starting later would conceal the denominator.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 955–1027 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The category distinction identifies the disputed remainder after spelling, nonsense readings, and readings confined to a single witness are removed.

burdenContact.rationale: This narrows the con significance burden to variants that are both possible and consequential rather than treating every copied difference alike.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: The earliest witnesses display multiple intersecting transmission lines rather than one centrally edited chain.
moves.warrant: White says varied lines and the absence of a controlling editor make coordinated wholesale alteration less plausible.
moves.inference: Distributed transmission supplies independent comparative evidence for reconstruction.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1029–1055 contain White’s early-witness count claim, the multiple-line inference, and the no-central-control consequence, ending before the distinct P75 illustration.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1029–1055 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: Independent early transmission lines without a central editor are White’s reason that agreement among geographically separated witnesses can preserve an ancient reading.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con recovery by offering independent transmission lines as evidence that no central authority could uniformly rewrite the text.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Representative printed Byzantine and critical texts agree on more than 95 percent of words.
moves.warrant: White distinguishes printed texts from manuscripts and reports under 6,600 differences.
moves.inference: Representative textual forms retain substantial continuity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1091–1155 contain the printed-edition limitation, samples, difference figure, and inference; removing one would blur the denominator.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1091–1155 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: The comparison between representative Byzantine and critical New Testament editions measures how much wording differs between two prominent reconstructed textual forms.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports the con continuity route by using two representative New Testament printed editions to quantify how much of their wording agrees.

moves.speaker: James White
moves.claim: Once a reading enters the manuscript tradition it tends to persist, including errors and nonsense readings.
moves.warrant: White uses textual tenacity and the extra-puzzle-pieces analogy to argue that original readings remain among surviving alternatives.
moves.inference: Reconstruction usually selects among extant readings rather than inventing a missing option.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1156–1204 state the persistence premise, draw the inference to surviving originals, give the puzzle analogy, and distinguish that claim from an absolute-certainty standard.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1156–1204 to James White’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Tenacity is a separate preservation premise: once readings enter the manuscript stream, they tend to persist, leaving later critics evidence to compare rather than erasing alternatives.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports con recovery because persistent readings remain available for comparison even after competitors arise.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Whether Mark says Jesus became angry or felt compassion creates a real local interpretive difference.
moves.warrant: Ehrman contrasts the two emotions while placing the example among a limited set of consequential variants.
moves.inference: The reading affects how Mark portrays Jesus at that episode.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1711–1718 state the complete anger-versus-love contrast and Ehrman’s conclusion that the difference is substantive; later exchanges supply, rather than replace, its evidential defense.
moves.attributionRationale: The source notes assign events 1711–1718 to Bart Ehrman’s uninterrupted formal speech; no opponent interjection contributes to the scored claim.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: The anger/compassion variant changes Jesus’ portrayed emotion and therefore supplies a focused test of whether a single-word variant can matter to interpretation.

burdenContact.rationale: This supports pro significance with a variant that changes the described mental state of Jesus.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: Ehrman’s former inspiration view became difficult because some original wording was uncertain.
moves.warrant: He says a God ensuring authors’ words could ensure preservation, while calling this personal rather than the main point.
moves.inference: For his former theology, uncertainty counted against verbal inspiration.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 1841–1892 preserve both the preservation argument and Ehrman’s explicit limitation that it is personal motivation rather than the central textual burden.
moves.attributionRationale: Events 1841–1891 are Ehrman’s closing portion of the rebuttal; event 1892 supplies his final word “yes” before White begins, and only Ehrman’s words are credited.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.
moves.importanceRationale: Ehrman’s former inerrancy doctrine explains the actual standard he says the evidence defeated: divine inspiration without exact preservation no longer secured the words.

burdenContact.rationale: This supplies the pro standard bridge: exact wording mattered because Ehrman’s inspiration doctrine treated the original words as divinely given.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: White’s claimed number of manuscripts within a century is not established by the examples and dating offered in cross-examination.
moves.warrant: Ehrman asks for the twelve witnesses; White cites Wallace, Comfort, Skeat, P52 and P32 but does not supply the complete list, and the dating remains contested.
moves.inference: The asserted early-witness quantity cannot carry more weight than its stated support in this debate.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2281–2373 retain the exact numerical question, White’s cited basis and examples, Ehrman’s dating challenge, and the immediate correction from 200 to 120; shortening it would remove a necessary qualification.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage alternates speakers. Ehrman owns the requests for the twelve manuscripts, the dating objections, and the correction challenge; White’s citations and numerical correction are retained only as the answers being tested.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The count or dating characterization follows the supplied transcript and source notes; no recognition-corrupted numeral or name is used beyond the qualified premise stated here.
moves.importanceRationale: The scarcity of very early witnesses directly tests whether later numerical abundance can establish what the first copies said.

burdenContact.rationale: This challenges con recovery at its weakest chronological point: the relative lack of witnesses close to the originals.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.claim: A word-agreement figure for representative printed editions is different from agreement among individual manuscripts at variant units.
moves.warrant: The cross-examination distinguishes printed reconstructed texts, individual manuscript collations, total words, and percentages used to group manuscripts.
moves.inference: The 95 percent figure cannot be transferred unchanged to a different evidence type or denominator.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Events 2375–2478 are needed because the parties repeatedly clarify what is being compared; the complete exchange preserves White’s printed-text limitation and Ehrman’s distinct manuscript question.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage alternates speakers. Ehrman owns the manuscript-versus-printed-text and variant-unit-versus-all-word questions; White’s repeated printed-text clarification is context and receives no pro credit.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct audio listening occurred. The claim is paraphrased from the supplied transcript and source notes, and no recognition-corrupted token is load-bearing.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest affirmative case is that religion should count as a conditional social technology whose institutions, narratives, and obligations can produce substantial welfare and reconciliation when constrained by pluralism, accountability, and interpretive correction.
premises: Religious motivation can be causally relevant even when compassion is not exclusively religious, because multiple motives may jointly sustain costly, organized, and persistent service.
Benefits should be credited only where evidence shows that religious networks, commitments, legitimacy, or resources materially improve outcomes over realistic alternatives.
Harms should likewise be charged to religion whenever doctrine, sacred identity, or institutional authority independently increases coercion, obstruction, or resistance to correction.
Pluralist law, democratic supremacy, transparent governance, and protected dissent can reduce religious coercion without excluding believers or their organizations from public contribution.
Interfaith actors may possess unusual legitimacy, vocabulary, relationships, and access for resolving disputes in which sacred identity forms part of the conflict.
finalArgument.conclusion: Religion can therefore be judged a qualified force for good where its demonstrable welfare, motivational, and reconciliation effects exceed attributable harms under transparent, symmetric comparison.

newArguments.title: Institutional option value
newArguments.text: Religious institutions may retain social option value even when secular substitutes exist. Dense local networks, trusted leaders, recurring gatherings, buildings, volunteers, and cross-border affiliations can be activated quickly during disaster, displacement, or institutional collapse. The relevant comparison is not whether a secular organization could theoretically perform the same work, but whether equivalent capacity is actually available at the needed time and place. This contribution should be credited only when measured against realistic alternatives and reduced by any exclusion, proselytism, or policy harm produced by the same institution.

newArguments.title: Constraint-sensitive religious benefit
newArguments.text: The variability of religion's effects can itself support a conditional affirmative position. If accountable governance, protected dissent, historical interpretation, and interfaith competition reliably shift religious energy from coercion toward service, then the relevant public question becomes institutional design rather than wholesale acceptance or rejection. This approach accepts the negative case's mechanisms as genuine risks while arguing that risks can be constrained without discarding beneficial networks, identities, and motivations. Its empirical burden is demanding: it requires comparative evidence that the safeguards reduce attributable harms while preserving measurable benefits.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest negative case is that religion fails the favorable net-balance test when its distinctive authority mechanisms create substantial correctability and coercion costs while its principal goods remain reproducible through nonreligious institutions.
premises: Charity, solidarity, humility, consolation, and moral seriousness are genuine goods, but their appearance among believers does not establish either doctrinal truth or religious necessity.
Religion is distinctively hazardous where claims of divine authorization weaken ordinary mechanisms of revision, accountability, compromise, or equal civic standing.
Causal attribution should charge religion only for the incremental effect of doctrine, sacred identity, or religious institutions after political and economic causes are considered.
Secular replaceability requires demonstrated institutions, incentives, communities, and resources, not merely the conceptual possibility that nonbelievers can display the same virtues.
Governmental neutrality and protected private association allow religious practice while reducing the risk that any contested revelation acquires coercive public authority.
finalArgument.conclusion: Religion should not receive a favorable overall judgment unless its demonstrated incremental benefits exceed its distinctive authority, conflict, and correctability costs under realistic secular comparison.

newArguments.title: Correctability cost
newArguments.text: A central comparative cost is not simply that religious communities sometimes reach harmful conclusions, since every ideology can do so, but that divine authorization can make correction more expensive. When a policy is treated as sacred obligation, contrary evidence may be interpreted as temptation, disloyalty, or illegitimate external interference. The relevant evidence would compare similarly situated religious and secular institutions on response time, transparency, leadership replacement, and policy revision after demonstrated harm. If sacred authorization systematically delays correction, that delay is a distinctive social cost even when the original error was not uniquely religious.

newArguments.title: Pluralism without metaphysical settlement
newArguments.text: A secular constitutional order offers a coordination advantage because citizens need not settle incompatible metaphysical claims before cooperating. Public reasons, revisable evidence, equal legal standing, and voluntary association permit believers and nonbelievers to pursue shared welfare while retaining private disagreement. This does not show that secular citizens are morally superior or that religious organizations contribute nothing. It argues instead that coercive authority should rest on standards accessible to people across traditions. Where religious service is valuable, it can continue under these neutral rules; where revelation demands unequal treatment, neutrality supplies a principled barrier.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that Christian belief can remain intellectually credible and morally constructive when presented as a cumulative, publicly answerable interpretation whose doctrines are governed by restorative love and corrigible practice.
premises: Scientific inquiry addresses empirical structures exceptionally well, yet its methods do not by themselves settle every metaphysical, normative, or existential question relevant to a comprehensive worldview.

Christian credibility should therefore rest on a cumulative comparison involving historical claims, lived experience, moral coherence, explanatory integration, and responsiveness to suffering, rather than on a gap in science.

A defensible account of atonement can preserve individual responsibility by construing Christ's voluntary suffering as restorative solidarity that enables reconciliation without transferring guilt or deserved punishment.

Christ-centered interpretation is principled only if enemy-love, nonretaliation, equal human dignity, and restoration function as transparent criteria applicable even against favored institutions and inherited readings.

Claims that Christianity is morally constructive require evidence that communities institutionalize those criteria through accountability, protection of dissent, repudiation of coercion, and measurable reconciliation practices.
finalArgument.conclusion: Christian belief is consequently defensible as a contestable cumulative interpretation, and morally constructive where its institutions demonstrably embody restorative, noncoercive, and self-correcting norms.

newArguments.title: Public cumulative warrant
newArguments.text: Conceptual space for transcendence becomes intellectually relevant only when joined to a comparative case. Christianity can propose that historical testimony, the intelligibility of reason, objective moral experience, consciousness, and practices of reconciliation jointly fit a theistic narrative better than isolated naturalistic accounts. None of these considerations compels assent individually, and each remains open to secular explanation. Their legitimate role is cumulative: they can raise Christianity from bare possibility to a publicly discussable hypothesis whose credibility depends on comparative explanatory success and willingness to revise overstated claims.

newArguments.title: Institutional falsifiability of moral claims
newArguments.text: A religion's constructive character should be tested through practices capable of contradicting its own self-description. Christian institutions could publish standards measuring protection of dissenters, treatment of enemies, restitution after abuse, resistance to political violence, and independent investigation of authority. Persistent failure would count against claims that enemy-love governs the tradition in practice. Reliable performance would not prove theology true, but it would support the narrower moral claim that particular Christian norms can generate accountable structures rather than functioning only as admirable rhetoric.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that religious claims should receive confidence proportionate to publicly accessible evidence, while morality and political legitimacy should be grounded in revisable human reasons rather than asserted supernatural authority.
premises: An unexplained cosmic origin does not identify an intervening personal deity, authenticate a revelation, or establish detailed knowledge of supernatural intentions and commands.

Historical revelation claims must be assessed through ordinary standards concerning provenance, corroboration, alternative explanation, transmission, and consistency rather than receiving exemption because their subject is supernatural.

Solidarity and reciprocity explain substantial moral motivation, but secular justification becomes stronger when supplemented by impartial consistency, interests in avoiding suffering, and procedures permitting criticism by affected people.

Authority becomes objectionably coercive when its rules are unavoidable, insulated from reciprocal challenge, extended to thought, and backed by disproportionate punishment, regardless of whether adherents describe submission as voluntary.

Religion's moral effects must be compared with secular institutions using disaggregated historical evidence, distinguishing doctrine, organization, political alliance, social conditions, and independent ideological causes.
finalArgument.conclusion: Confidence in specific religious doctrines should remain limited without adequate public warrant, and shared moral and political rules should remain open to reciprocal criticism without dependence on inaccessible divine authorization.

newArguments.title: Reciprocal accessibility standard
newArguments.text: Public moral rules should be justifiable through reasons that people with different metaphysical commitments can inspect, challenge, and revise. This does not make theological reasons meaningless to believers; it limits their authority over nonconsenting others unless translated into considerations such as preventable harm, equal standing, or fair cooperation. The standard addresses coercion more precisely than a broad totalitarian analogy because it identifies the defect as asymmetrical accountability: citizens may question one another, whereas an asserted divine command can be presented as beyond reciprocal correction while still governing everyone.

newArguments.title: From cooperation to obligation
newArguments.text: A secular moral account can move beyond evolutionary genealogy by combining three claims: conscious beings have interests in avoiding suffering and preserving agency; consistency requires comparable interests to receive comparable consideration; and fair procedures allow everyone affected to contest partial applications. Evolution helps explain why humans can recognize and act on these reasons, but it does not create their authority. Their normative force comes from impartial treatment of interests and reciprocal accountability, including when helping outsiders is costly. This framework remains revisable, yet revision is a strength because errors can be exposed without appealing to inaccessible revelation.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman for The Church is a force for good combines the side's strongest recorded claims into a measured case that directly answers the clearest objection raised in the debate.
premises: The case's strongest foundation is this recorded point: Onaiyekan grounded the affirmative case in substantial, identifiable medical, educational, refugee, and welfare provision.
A second supporting consideration is this recorded point: Widdecombe correctly challenged overbroad inferences from celibacy and demanded greater precision about doctrine and historical context.

The cumulative case also gains support from this recorded point: The team showed that Catholic service is often delivered across creedal boundaries and that public-health policy is more complex than a single intervention.

The strengthened position must directly answer this recorded limitation: Widdecombe diverted the institutional-abuse charge toward unrelated secular failures without answering Catholic secrecy and offender-protection mechanisms.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, The Church is a force for good is supported only insofar as this combined case explains the debate's central evidence better than its rival while surviving the stated limitation.

newArguments.title: Comparative prediction test
newArguments.text: A stronger version would turn the motion into a comparison of expectations. The The Church is a force for good side should identify which observations are more likely if its account is correct, which are more likely under the rival account, and what evidence would change the conclusion. Applied to the question—Is the Catholic Church, considered as an institution and global social force, a force for good in the world?—this approach replaces isolated possibility claims with a cumulative test and prevents one attractive example from carrying the entire case.

newArguments.title: Objection stress test
newArguments.text: The case can gain credibility by adopting its opponent's strongest pressure point: Widdecombe diverted the institutional-abuse charge toward unrelated secular failures without answering Catholic secrecy and offender-protection mechanisms. Rather than dismissing that concern, the side should state a specific repair, acknowledge what remains uncertain, and describe how an observer could distinguish its explanation from the leading alternatives. A conclusion that survives this stress test is stronger because it shows where the argument could fail and why the available evidence still favors it.
