finalArgument.thesis: Theism gains comparative support if one integrated personal foundation can nonnecessitatingly ground contingent reality while also making calibrated religious awareness and culturally mediated relationship more expected than they are under naturalism.
premises: A satisfactory comparison should reward not merely the availability of separate explanations but also explanatory integration across contingency, consciousness, normativity, religious awareness, and interpersonal significance.
Divine freedom should be offered as a model of nonnecessitating determination only after theism explains how reasons can guide creation without causally compelling one uniquely necessary history.
An essence-based terminus has comparative value only if a substantive account of perfect agency constrains the divine nature more tightly than a merely nominated natural initial state.

Religious experience should contribute through a calibrated cumulative case using cross-context coherence, durable moral transformation, resistance to expectation, and responsible testimonial transmission rather than intensity alone.

Religious diversity is compatible with divine relationship only if theism states limited communicative aims and identifies observable patterns that cultural mediation predicts without making every possible distribution equally expected.
finalArgument.conclusion: If the personal-grounding model supplies genuine integration, survives symmetry, and supports independently calibrated experiential expectations, theism receives a meaningful but defeasible overall explanatory advantage over naturalism.

newArguments.title: Cross-domain compression
newArguments.text: A personal ground could earn comparative value through cross-domain compression rather than by filling a single unexplained gap. If the same constrained account of perfect agency helps explain why contingent reality exists, why rational creatures can recognize reasons, and why interpersonal or religious awareness arises, its cost is not simply one extra entity repeated across several arguments. The relevant test is whether the shared structure yields independent expectations and fewer disconnected primitives than the best naturalistic package. This argument succeeds only if those expectations are stated beforehand and cannot be recreated equally well by unrelated natural mechanisms.

newArguments.title: Costly counterexpectational experience
newArguments.text: Religious evidence could be filtered for experiences that are costly, resistant to prior expectation, stable under reflection, and productive of specific long-term changes not easily explained by conformity or immediate reward. Such cases would not automatically verify their theological interpretation, but they could receive more weight than raw prevalence or subjective intensity. Comparing these markers across traditions would also expose rather than conceal disagreement. Theism would gain support only if the selected pattern is more expected under limited divine relational aims than under independently specified psychological and social mechanisms.

finalArgument.thesis: Naturalism is comparatively preferable when natural foundational models match theism's metaphysical possibilities and independently grounded cognitive, cultural, and historical mechanisms better predict the distribution of religious belief and experience.
premises: Comparative judgment should use shared criteria including explanatory scope, predictive constraint, integration, ontological commitment, and sensitivity to evidence rather than treating simplicity or coverage as self-interpreting virtues.

A necessary natural foundation with indeterministic development is a legitimate modal countermodel, although naturalism should distinguish demonstrating coherence from providing a complete explanation of why that structure obtains.
No essence-based stopping rule favors God unless independently warranted divine content explains necessity more successfully than an equally constrained account of fundamental natural reality.

Religious experiences require calibration using mechanisms, base conditions, cross-tradition disagreement, situational reliability, and differences between confidence that an experience occurred and confidence in its supernatural interpretation.

Naturalism gains comparative support if independently evidenced learning, agency detection, prestige transmission, institutional selection, and historical isolation jointly predict both recurring religious themes and durable doctrinal divergence.
finalArgument.conclusion: If these mechanisms predict the evidence with greater constraint while theistic grounding and communication remain symmetrically available but weakly differentiated, naturalism earns a defeasible comparative advantage.

newArguments.title: Mechanism portability test
newArguments.text: Naturalistic explanations should be tested for portability beyond religion. If ordinary mechanisms such as agency detection, memory reconstruction, prestige learning, coalition signaling, and institutional selection already explain comparable patterns in political, moral, paranormal, and ideological belief, applying them to religion gains independent support. Portability reduces the danger of inventing a mechanism solely to dismiss religious evidence. The comparison should still examine residual features that these mechanisms fail to predict. Naturalism gains ground only where independently evidenced processes forecast both common experiential structures and culturally variable interpretations without ad hoc adjustment.

newArguments.title: Asymmetric prediction ledger
newArguments.text: The worldviews can be compared through a preregistered ledger of divergent expectations: the frequency of unsolicited experiences, their dependence on training, rates of doctrinal convergence, correction after contradictory revelation, geographic inheritance, and persistence under social disruption. Neither worldview should receive credit merely for accommodating results afterward. A naturalistic package gains support where established mechanisms assign the observed patterns higher prior likelihood than a specified relational-divine model. Conversely, convergence or reliable novel information could count against that package. This framework converts communicative disorder from an intuitive complaint into a balanced program of discriminating comparisons.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest defensible pro case is that several partially independent features make substantial historical preservation across the canonical Gospels more probable, without claiming equal certainty for every saying, event, or theological formulation.
premises: Integrated Palestinian geography, measures, idiom, travel patterns, and personal-name distributions are evidence that the traditions or their sources were connected to informed local knowledge.
Locally informed access does not prove every narrative, but it is more expected if some substantial early tradition was preserved than if the accounts were freely invented in detached settings.
Mark's exalted characterization and the Synoptic precedents for Johannine themes weaken a model in which high claims about Jesus emerged without meaningful continuity from earlier traditions.

Apparent discrepancies should reduce confidence in the disputed details proportionately, but a plausible reconciliation can prevent a contradiction from being treated as demonstrated solely by narrative compression.

A cumulative inference is strongest when each indicator is assigned only its local evidential reach and when dependence among contextual, literary, and theological indicators is explicitly discounted.
finalArgument.conclusion: Taken together, these considerations support qualified historical confidence in substantial Gospel preservation, while leaving individual reports, exact wording, harmonizations, and resurrection claims open to separate evidential examination.

newArguments.title: Error-Distribution Test
newArguments.text: A preservation model can be strengthened by comparing where errors and agreements occur. If the Gospels repeatedly agree on difficult, locally embedded, and causally connected details while diverging more often in peripheral chronology, compression, or narrative perspective, that distribution would be more informative than a raw count of agreements. The pro case should therefore predict a structured pattern: stable central contours with variable secondary presentation. This is a genuinely new test because it specifies what differentiated reliability would look like and permits the model to fail if consequential claims display no greater stability than incidental ones.

newArguments.title: Rival-Model Likelihood Matrix
newArguments.text: Instead of treating Palestinian knowledge as direct proof, the pro side could compare four hypotheses: eyewitness composition, early informed sources, later competent research, and mixed transmission. Each observed feature would receive a likelihood under every hypothesis, with dependence discounts for features arising from the same source. Personal-name frequencies may distinguish detached invention from local information, whereas literary coherence may distinguish little at all. The combined result could support early informed tradition without overclaiming authorship or universal accuracy. This framework answers the setting-event criticism by making every inferential step comparative, transparent, and limited to what each feature can diagnose.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest defensible con case is that the canonical Gospels contain historically valuable traditions but require claim-specific evaluation because provenance uncertainty, transmission pathways, narrative tensions, and source development affect propositions differently.
premises: Decades between events and final compositions, cross-language transmission, uncertain authorship, and unnamed intermediaries reduce direct access confidence even though none of those factors alone demonstrates corruption.

Accurate contextual information supports informed provenance, yet it cannot establish the truth of particular sayings or events unless a further connection between source access and content preservation is demonstrated.

The Judas accounts impose a concrete evidential cost because a successful reconciliation must jointly explain death mechanism, sequence, purchaser, and field-name rationale rather than supplementing only one detail.
Early exalted narration and later explicit self-claims may exhibit conceptual continuity while still differing historically in wording, speaker attribution, frequency, and theological emphasis.

Historical confidence should therefore vary by proposition according to source multiplicity, independence, genre, transmission exposure, internal tension, and corroboration rather than inheriting a single verdict from each Gospel.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, the evidence supports selective historical recovery from the Gospels but does not justify treating the canonical accounts as uniformly reliable across disputed events, exact sayings, and developed identity claims.

newArguments.title: Claim-Level Reliability Grid
newArguments.text: The con side could replace a global reliability verdict with a structured grid. Each claim would be classified by attestation, source independence, genre, linguistic distance, theological loading, and compatibility with parallel accounts. Widely attested public events might receive substantial confidence, whereas exact private sayings or reports appearing only in a later theological narrative would require more caution. This method prevents one discrepancy from contaminating everything and prevents accurate geography from certifying everything. It is a new reinforcing argument because it converts general revisability into a transparent procedure capable of producing both positive and negative historical conclusions.

newArguments.title: Harmonization Complexity Penalty
newArguments.text: When two reports differ, logical compatibility should be separated from historical probability. A reconciliation that adds several unattested events, agency conventions, temporal stages, or causal links may remain possible, yet each added element increases explanatory complexity. The relevant comparison is therefore not contradiction versus any imaginable reconciliation, but the relative likelihood of a unified sequence against distinct or altered traditions. Applied to Judas, the hanging-then-fall proposal addresses one dimension while purchaser and field-name explanations require additional work. This approach strengthens the con case without assuming that every textual difference is irreconcilable.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that textual trust is warranted when multiple partially independent forms of evidence make substantial recovery more probable than relevant alternatives, even though some readings and the exact autograph relationship remain uncertain.
premises: Branching witnesses, versions, patristic citations, and internal scribal patterns can provide convergent constraints whose force depends on genealogy and independence rather than on manuscript quantity alone.

The ability to identify conspicuous later additions and classify most differences as accidental is evidence that comparative criticism can detect at least many significant departures within the observable tradition.

An ancestral text need not be proven identical to an autograph for historically responsible trust if the remaining hypotheses of shared early alteration are constrained and do not dominate the cumulative evidence.
Trust should be disaggregated: confidence may be high for broad wording, lower at disclosed disputed readings, and undecided where the evidence cannot discriminate among viable alternatives.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, the surviving evidence can justify qualified trust in substantial New Testament wording while requiring explicit uncertainty at contested readings and withholding certainty about complete autographic identity.

newArguments.title: Detection as a method check
newArguments.text: Known substantial additions are not only evidence of scribal change; their identification also functions as a limited performance check on textual criticism. When early witnesses, distribution patterns, and internal considerations converge to mark a passage as secondary, the method demonstrates an ability to detect consequential growth rather than merely assuming stability. This does not show that every early alteration is recoverable, but it weakens the claim that the existence of important additions by itself defeats qualified trust in the critically reconstructed text.

newArguments.title: Portfolio confidence model
newArguments.text: Textual trust can be modeled as a portfolio of local judgments rather than a single all-or-nothing proposition. Readings supported across early, independent, and geographically dispersed channels receive greater confidence; genealogically dependent or internally ambiguous readings receive less. The aggregate claim of substantial recovery then rests on the distribution of confidence across locations, with disputed passages openly flagged. This model would require transparent criteria and empirical application, but it prevents a small number of difficult readings from automatically determining confidence in every other location.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that substantial reconstruction of the surviving tradition does not alone warrant confidence in authorial wording unless evidence also constrains consequential alterations before the earliest recoverable branching point.
premises: Comparison among descendants can recover their common ancestor while remaining structurally unable to expose a change already present in every descendant before their divergence.
The absence of early copies does not prove corruption, but it widens uncertainty precisely where a consequential alteration could become ancestral to all surviving witness families.
Observed substantial additions establish that influential textual growth occurred, while their successful detection shows only that some changes after evidentiary branching remain recoverable.

A probabilistic trust claim requires sensitivity analysis showing that reasonable assumptions about undocumented early copying do not materially change the conclusion of substantial authorial recovery.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, broad continuity may be historically probable while confidence in substantial autographic recovery remains conditional until the case demonstrates robustness against plausible shared alterations in the undocumented earliest period.

newArguments.title: Shared-error blind spot
newArguments.text: Branching reconstruction is strongest for errors introduced after branches separate, because disagreement among descendants creates information about their ancestor. Its evidentiary leverage is weaker for an alteration already fixed before the surviving branches diverged. The relevant question is therefore not whether comparison works, but where the recoverable branching point lies relative to authorial composition and how much opportunity existed before it. Unless that temporal relationship is constrained, excellent reconstruction of a common ancestor can coexist with unresolved uncertainty about the autograph.

newArguments.title: Robustness under early-change scenarios
newArguments.text: A stronger evaluation would test the pro conclusion across explicit early-transmission scenarios: careful copying with dispersed exemplars, mixed-quality copying with rapid branching, and a bottleneck in which one altered exemplar dominates later witnesses. The point is not to assume the worst scenario, but to ask whether available evidence discriminates among them and whether substantial recovery remains likely across the plausible range. If the conclusion depends heavily on an unverified favorable scenario, the appropriate confidence should remain conditional even while broad continuity is conceded.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest traditional-authorship case is a comparative hypothesis: early attribution, text-specific fit, and historically bounded mediation jointly favor connections to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John without requiring unaided autograph composition by every namesake.
premises: External witnesses should contribute weight only to the extent that their chronology, geography, canonical-text identification, and probable information channels are distinguishable rather than merely repetitive.
Internal evidence need not uniquely identify an author to matter, but each feature must be shown more expected under the traditional connection than under an anonymous source, editor, or narrator.

Mediated authorship should require a stable division of labor specifying whether the traditional figure supplied testimony, selected sources, supervised translation, authorized publication, or performed composition.
Mark and Luke can count against simplistic prestige-maximizing invention only after comparing direct-apostle naming with the rival strategy of representing Peter and Paul through associates.

Formal biographical anonymity is evidentially neutral only when independent attribution information plausibly accompanied circulation; therefore early canonical identification remains indispensable to the traditional hypothesis.
finalArgument.conclusion: If the attribution channels prove partly independent, the internal features supply comparative rather than merely compatible support, and mediated roles are historically specified, traditional connections become a reasonable explanation without claiming certainty about every final composer's identity.

newArguments.title: Attribution Network Test
newArguments.text: The traditional case could model each witness as a node in an attribution network and ask what information route best explains the agreement. Geographic separation matters only if communities had partially independent access to titles, teachers, manuscripts, or memories. Evidence of cross-dependence would reduce the multiplication of testimony, while evidence that a canonical text and its name traveled together before later controversies would increase it. This approach turns a loose appeal to diversity into a testable comparison between inherited identification and diffusion of a single later convention.

newArguments.title: Role-Specific Authorship Matrix
newArguments.text: Rather than treating authorship as one undifferentiated act, the case could compare five roles for each Gospel: eyewitness source, oral transmitter, source selector, literary composer, and publication authority. The traditional claim would then succeed only for roles supported by evidence, allowing Mark's Petrine source relationship or a possible Matthean authorization model to be assessed without automatically identifying the final stylist. This matrix answers the identity objection by making the asserted connection precise and prevents assistance from expanding opportunistically whenever a linguistic difficulty appears.

finalArgument.thesis: The strongest anonymous-authorship case is that the available evidence underdetermines the traditional identities: textual anonymity, literary capacity, and later naming are better explained without positing direct composition or demonstrated authorization by the four namesakes.
premises: Narrative anonymity does not prove universal ignorance, but it lowers identification confidence when no securely early paratext, self-reference, or independent community testimony connects a canonical text to its later namesake.
First-person travel, privileged access, and disciple rosters can indicate sources or narrators without identifying final composers, so every transition between those roles requires separate evidence.

Educational mismatch is strongest against personal Greek composition and weaker against authorization; accordingly, the negative case should demand evidence for authorization rather than assuming illiteracy excludes every mediated relationship.

A later naming hypothesis gains credibility from institutional incentives and strategically coherent names, but it should remain a comparative explanation unless direct evidence establishes a coordinated assignment event.

Stable unanimity has evidential value, yet Barnabas and Second Clement demonstrate that conventional attribution can remain stable; chronology and independence must therefore determine how much weight unanimity receives.
finalArgument.conclusion: Unless early attribution channels, internal identity indicators, or historically evidenced mediation connect the namesakes to specific texts, anonymous educated composition followed by conventional attribution remains the more economical explanation, though the precise naming event may remain uncertain.

newArguments.title: Evidence-Risk Asymmetry
newArguments.text: The two hypotheses do not incur the same evidential risks. Traditional authority predicts some discoverable identity-specific connection between a namesake and the canonical text, whereas anonymous composition can accommodate reliable traditions, eyewitness sources, and later stable titles without identifying the final author. Consequently, evidence for reliability should be credited equally under both hypotheses unless it specifically favors the named figure. This comparison explains why generally plausible transmission mechanisms do not close the attribution gap while avoiding the stronger assertion that reliable apostolic material is absent.

newArguments.title: Paratext Survival Comparison
newArguments.text: The negative case could compare how titles, incipits, subscriptions, citations, and catalog entries survive for other ancient works across manuscript families. If author names normally travel early and consistently with known works, their delayed secure appearance for the Gospels becomes more significant; if labels are commonly lost or unstable, the inference weakens. The value lies in establishing an external baseline instead of reasoning from silence alone. Such a comparison would make the anonymity argument empirically discriminating and clarify what surviving evidence each hypothesis should predict.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that resurrection merits serious comparative preference only if a carefully delimited factual core is established and that core is substantially more expected under divine bodily resurrection than under the strongest integrated alternatives.
premises: Early testimony supports at least sincere postmortem experiences among named individuals and groups, even though the precise phenomenology and bodily character of those experiences require separate argument.

Burial and empty-tomb traditions should contribute only in proportion to their demonstrated dating, independence, and resistance to plausible literary-development accounts, rather than being treated as uniformly settled facts.

The unexpected emergence of individualized resurrection belief has evidentiary force when assessed against specifically documented expectations, while still allowing that reinterpretation and visionary experience could transform prior commitments.

A valid comparison must evaluate posterior probability through the expectedness of the evidence under resurrection and under the strongest naturalistic packages, not merely invoke either low priors or explanatory unity.

Religious-historical context may discriminate among supernatural interpretations only where the contextual claims are independently supported and the comparison does not presuppose the intended divine identification.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, resurrection can be defended as a serious and potentially preferable explanation, but preference is warranted only to the extent that the restricted factual core and comparative likelihood claims withstand source-critical and underdetermination challenges.

newArguments.title: Correlated-evidence comparison
newArguments.text: The evidence should not be counted as four independent confirmations if burial, emptiness, appearances, and belief development share sources or causal pathways. Instead, construct competing causal models and ask which predicts the observed combination with fewer unsupported auxiliary assumptions. Resurrection gains comparative force only if the joint pattern is appreciably less expected under carefully specified vision, removal, and development models, after source dependence is incorporated.

newArguments.title: Risky-prediction test
newArguments.text: A stronger resurrection case would identify features that its hypothesis predicts before consulting each disputed tradition, then test whether alternatives predict those same features equally well. Candidate features might include the timing, social distribution, embodied interpretation, and persistence of experiences. This prevents explanatory flexibility from turning every possible record into confirmation and supplies a clearer standard for comparing resurrection with composite naturalistic accounts.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that historical evidence does not warrant selecting divine bodily resurrection when the factual core is source-contested, accessible developmental models remain viable, and supernatural agency cannot be uniquely identified by shared evidence.
premises: Source limitations should reduce confidence claim by claim: generic burial, Joseph's identity, tomb discovery, appearance occurrence, and embodied interpretation require separate evaluations rather than one global reliability verdict.

Reports of postmortem experiences establish neither their external cause nor their bodily ontology without additional evidence that discriminates visions, memory development, literary elaboration, and embodied encounters.

Low prior probability alone cannot exclude resurrection; the stronger objection is that the available evidence does not yield stable, publicly defensible likelihoods sufficient to overcome uncertainty about sources and divine agency.

Natural scenarios need not be proven as the actual history to defeat comparative uniqueness; they must be sufficiently specified and evidentially viable to show that the record remains materially underdetermined.

Context can rank narratives provisionally, but it cannot by itself establish which supernatural agent acted or whether apparent contextual fit was produced by later interpretation of ambiguous experiences.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, the proportionate historical conclusion is suspended comparative judgment: the evidence may support early resurrection belief and reported experiences without establishing divine bodily resurrection as the uniquely best historical explanation.

newArguments.title: Identification gap
newArguments.text: Even if the evidence strongly favored an extraordinary external cause, an additional identification step would remain. The historian would need evidence distinguishing the God of the Christian proclamation from unknown agency, deception, anomalous natural processes, or rival supernatural accounts. Context can alter comparative plausibility, but the identification evidence must be independently supported rather than inferred solely from the event it is invoked to explain.

newArguments.title: Retrospective-fit control
newArguments.text: Religious context may look highly predictive after communities have interpreted events through inherited scriptures and subsequently shaped their narratives around those interpretations. A historical comparison should therefore separate contextual claims demonstrably preceding the experiences from motifs documented only in later accounts. If the strongest fit emerges chiefly in later narration, contextual coherence may reflect retrospective construction rather than independent confirmation of resurrection.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that bodily resurrection merits acceptance as the best historical explanation only if a carefully qualified cumulative case makes death, bodily absence, early embodied belief, and appearances jointly more expected than they are under the strongest nonresurrection alternatives.
premises: Roman execution practice, the preceding trauma, early death proclamation, and the reported official confirmation should be treated as mutually relevant but not automatically independent evidence, yielding a strong case-specific probability of death without invoking universal medical agreement.

The empty tomb should rest on a cumulative assessment of burial identification, Jerusalem proclamation, hostile body-removal explanation, and embodied resurrection semantics, with each indicator discounted where its provenance or dependence remains uncertain.

Early appearance testimony most securely establishes sincere and transformative experiences; a bodily interpretation becomes stronger only when that testimony is combined with embodied resurrection language and bodily absence, not from sincerity or conversion alone.

Early Pauline and pre-Pauline formulas should be cited individually and evaluated for dating, provenance, and bodily meaning; chronology supports the case only when the formulas themselves connect the deceased Jesus with the one proclaimed raised.

Explanatory comparison should test resurrection, survival, rescue, bereavement or revelatory experiences, spiritual vindication, and narrative development by common criteria: coverage, evidential fit, auxiliary assumptions, source chronology, and compatibility with acknowledged uncertainty.
finalArgument.conclusion: If the death, bodily-absence, early embodied-belief, and appearance strands retain substantial support after dependence and source development are discounted, bodily resurrection can be judged the strongest presented explanation, though the historical inference remains probabilistic and contestable.

newArguments.title: Correlated-evidence sensitivity test
newArguments.text: A stronger affirmative case would explicitly model evidential dependence. The hostile explanation may depend on the same tradition as the empty-tomb narrative, and bodily resurrection semantics may not independently prove a known burial place. The case should therefore ask whether its conclusion survives after correlated indicators receive reduced weight. If death, bodily absence, early proclamation, and sincere appearances still converge after that discount, the inference gains credibility precisely because it does not depend on counting every report as independent confirmation.

newArguments.title: Discriminating-predictions comparison
newArguments.text: Rather than claiming that every alternative fails, the affirmative could identify observations on which the accounts differ. Survival predicts a severely injured continuing Jesus and requires a pathway through custody; purely visionary accounts do not naturally predict bodily absence; pure literary development weakens expectations of a very early identified resurrection proclamation. None of those contrasts is decisive alone, but jointly they permit a transparent comparison. Resurrection earns preference only if it predicts the combined pattern with fewer unsupported auxiliary assumptions than each serious rival.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that the historical record can support early sincere resurrection belief while still failing to discriminate sufficiently between physical resurrection and combinations of uncertain death, revelatory experience, spiritual vindication, and later narrative physicalization.
premises: The death premise should be evaluated cumulatively, but Mark's rapid timeline, Pilate's reported surprise, and the later emergence of decisive physical details leave some case-specific uncertainty that general crucifixion lethality alone cannot remove.

Early resurrection language may have bodily associations without itself documenting an identifiable empty tomb, numerical continuity with the corpse, or tactile encounters; those propositions require separate historical bridges rather than semantic assumption.

Paul's placement of his revelatory experience beside earlier appearances does not prove identical phenomenology, but it demonstrates that list membership alone cannot establish that every recipient encountered a tangible, locally present body.

Increasing physical specificity across later narratives is evidence of development only after literary dependence, genre, authorial purpose, and possible clarification are assessed; nevertheless, it limits using later detail as straightforward independent confirmation.

Historical non-establishment does not require proving a complete rescue or survival narrative; it requires showing that key evidence has similar likelihood under multiple live accounts after reasonable uncertainty and source dependence are recognized.
finalArgument.conclusion: Unless the evidence independently secures death, bodily absence, and specifically physical appearances while distinguishing early content from later elaboration, the proportionate historical conclusion is that bodily resurrection remains insufficiently established, not that a particular alternative is proved.

newArguments.title: Incremental-content audit
newArguments.text: The negative could separate the tradition into propositions and date the earliest secure support for each: Jesus died, God raised him, appearances were reported, the burial place was empty, and encounters involved tangible bodily interaction. Early support for the first three would not automatically backdate the final two. This incremental audit avoids treating every later detail as invention while still asking whether the evidence needed for physical resurrection appears only after additional narrative development. The motion fails if its distinctively physical components remain later or independently uncertain.

newArguments.title: Likelihood-equivalence challenge
newArguments.text: The negative need not show that one naturalistic theory explains everything. It can ask whether crucial observations are approximately as expected under more than one account: sincere experiences under revelation or grief, early raising language under vindication, and increasing physical detail under clarification or development. Where rival accounts predict an observation comparably well, that observation contributes little discriminatory force. The affirmative must therefore identify evidence whose probability differs materially across the alternatives, rather than relying primarily on the number or vividness of mutually compatible facts.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that bodily resurrection is a rational best explanation only if an early, multiply constrained historical core is more expected under purposeful divine action than under the strongest combined natural alternatives.
premises: The earliest recoverable tradition should be separated from later narrative elaboration, with only death, burial or body disposition, appearance claims, and the conversions of James and Paul entering the initial explanatory core.

Bodily interpretation gains support only to the extent that distinct traditions converge on tangible continuity, transformation, identification, and interaction without their agreement being adequately explained by dependence or literary development.

Natural alternatives should be compared in their strongest combined form, with grief experience, individual visions, body removal, memory development, and social reinforcement assessed for fit rather than rejected merely because several mechanisms are required.

Miracle attribution requires an independently defensible theistic background and contextual evidence connecting the alleged event to Jesus' claims, while the event may reciprocally update but cannot singlehandedly manufacture that theology.

If the restricted historical core is substantially more expected under resurrection than under the strongest combined alternatives, even after conservative source and prior-probability adjustments, resurrection can be rational without becoming certain.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, the historical evidence can make bodily resurrection rational as a best explanation, but only conditionally on source independence, bodily convergence, comparative likelihood, and agent-specific theological warrant surviving detailed scrutiny.

newArguments.title: Discriminating-evidence matrix
newArguments.text: Construct an explicit matrix listing each datum and its expectedness under bodily resurrection, grief visions, individual hallucination, body removal, legendary development, and combined natural accounts. Source dependence should reduce the weight of correlated reports, while unexpected conversions and independently supported bodily details receive only the weight their provenance permits. This method improves the affirmative case because it does not rely on counting hypotheses or repeating that resurrection is unified; it identifies which evidence actually discriminates among explanations and displays where the conclusion remains sensitive to disputed historical judgments.

newArguments.title: Reciprocal contextual updating
newArguments.text: Treat background theism and the alleged resurrection as mutually updating but evidentially nonidentical. Prior arguments for God, the historical setting of Jesus' claims, and expectations within Mosaic theism can make purposeful divine action less arbitrary; independently supported resurrection evidence can then increase confidence that those contextual claims were authentically significant. Neither component may simply assume the other. The resulting structure answers the demand for agent and intention while avoiding the unsupported shortcut that any extraordinary return from death would automatically endorse every theological proposition associated with the person.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that bodily resurrection is not historically established when source dependence, incomplete bodily evidence, credible ordinary possibility, and uncertain agent-specific theology leave the decisive likelihood comparison unresolved.
premises: Historical proximity does not equal independence: an early creed can establish early belief and transmission while leaving the experiences' exact content, verification, and relationship to later narratives uncertain.

The evidence for tangible embodiment must be discounted where contact is merely invited, reports are textually related, or sensory details may reflect later theological and literary clarification rather than independent observation.

Skepticism need not supply one complete replacement history; it must instead show that plausible combinations of visionary experience, social reinforcement, memory development, and body disposition prevent resurrection from becoming clearly superior.
A miraculous explanation requires not only an anomalous event but justified beliefs identifying a capable agent and a reason that this particular event would express that agent's intention.

When likelihood estimates depend heavily on contested source relationships and theological assumptions, suspension or a tentative natural interpretation can be rational without declaring resurrection impossible.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, the available evidence may support early resurrection belief and sincere experiences without making an externally tangible, divinely caused resurrection the uniquely warranted or sufficiently established historical conclusion.

newArguments.title: Dependence-sensitive underdetermination
newArguments.text: Model the resurrection evidence as a network rather than a list. If later bodily narratives depend directly or indirectly on an early proclamation, their agreement is not equivalent to multiple independent observations. Conversely, genuinely independent details should receive additional weight. Because the central historical dispute concerns precisely these relationships, a conclusion that remains highly sensitive to reasonable dependence assumptions is not securely established. This argument does not infer falsity from uncertainty; it identifies why apparent convergence may provide less discrimination than a simple accumulation of sources suggests.

newArguments.title: Agency-identification gap
newArguments.text: Even unusually strong evidence that a dead person appeared alive would initially support several propositions with different strengths: mistaken death diagnosis, survival, unusual natural occurrence, unknown agency, or purposeful divine action. Moving specifically to God's authentication of Jesus requires contextual evidence that distinguishes the final interpretation from the others and identifies intended meaning. The historical event may contribute to that case, but using the alleged resurrection simultaneously as proof of agency, intention, and authentication risks collapsing separate inferential stages. Keeping those stages distinct preserves openness to evidence while explaining why anomaly alone is insufficient.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that forgiveness through Christ can coherently unite mercy and justice when atonement is understood as God’s voluntary, representative self-giving that restores communion and produces transformed conduct.
premises: If moral law expresses God’s holy character, forgiveness should condemn wrongdoing and restore the offender through a stable principle rather than through unexplained discretionary remission.
Christ’s self-giving can avoid the unwilling-third-party objection if the acting subject is divine, voluntary, and representatively united with those whose condition he assumes.

Biblical sacrifice can function as a canonical pattern of purification, covenant restoration, and representative approach to God without requiring every metaphor to denote an identical commercial transaction.
Spirit-produced obedience can be necessary as the lived form and evidence of reconciliation while remaining distinct from the sufficient ground on which acceptance is given.

Claims of biblical continuity should rest on multiple converging strands—early Christian tradition, Jewish interpretive plurality, ritual patterns, and textual exegesis—rather than canonical assertion alone.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, Christ-centered forgiveness is coherent if voluntary divine representation supplies a principled restorative ground, scripture cumulatively supports that interpretation, and transformed deeds remain its necessary fruit rather than its purchase price.

newArguments.title: Restorative representation model
newArguments.text: A stronger account need not portray atonement as punishment mechanically moved from one unrelated individual to another. It can treat Christ as the voluntary representative who enters the human condition, publicly condemns sin through costly solidarity, and inaugurates restored covenant communion. This model still requires a defense of representation, but it explains why self-giving, resurrection, purification, and moral transformation belong together more naturally than the isolated image of an angry father harming an unwilling son.

newArguments.title: Convergent continuity test
newArguments.text: The pro case could test continuity through convergence rather than relying on canonical status by itself. It should ask whether early creedal material, pre-Pauline traditions, Jewish interpretive diversity, sacrificial institutions, Gospel sayings, and apostolic writings independently cluster around representative suffering and restoration. No single strand would settle the issue, but convergence would answer the development objection more effectively than broad appeals to inspiration, while remaining open to genuine theological development within an enduring core.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman is that direct divine forgiveness can coherently preserve justice when it operates through publicly intelligible standards of repentance, restitution, proportional accountability, moral rehabilitation, and equal mercy.
premises: Justice need not require suffering equivalent to every wrong if wrongdoing is truthfully condemned, victims’ claims are respected, repair is pursued, and offenders undergo accountable moral change.
Repentance is morally meaningful only when it includes acknowledgment, cessation, restitution where possible, and renewed conduct, so direct mercy need not amount to costless indulgence.
Biblical descriptions of imperfect people as righteous support a graded account of accountable faithfulness, even if they do not prove sinlessness or complete adequacy before perfect holiness.

Historical-development claims should be framed probabilistically and supported by specific redactional patterns, chronological evidence, and independently assessable changes rather than by later explicit wording alone.

New Testament commands, judgment passages, and works language can establish that participation is indispensable without requiring the stronger claim that good deeds mechanically earn divine acceptance.
finalArgument.conclusion: Accordingly, direct forgiveness is coherent if mercy follows substantive restorative principles, human participation remains enabled yet indispensable, and scriptural-development objections are argued through qualified historical evidence rather than categorical assertions.

newArguments.title: Restorative justice specification
newArguments.text: The con position can answer the charge of arbitrary pardon by offering a restorative decision structure: wrongdoing is named, victims retain moral standing, restitution is required where feasible, repentance must produce changed conduct, and final judgment remains proportionate to knowledge, opportunity, harm, and response. Mercy then concerns release from deserved condemnation after morally relevant transformation, not denial that law was violated. This approach gives direct forgiveness substantive content beyond treating similar offenders alike.

newArguments.title: Explanatory economy comparison
newArguments.text: A comparative coherence test can ask which account introduces fewer disputed mechanisms while preserving the shared data of guilt, repentance, mercy, justice, and transformed conduct. Direct forgiveness requires an account of principled remission, whereas substitution requires additional accounts of representation, transferred liability, imputed righteousness, and why suffering satisfies justice. This does not establish that substitution is false, but it gives the con side a disciplined comparative argument: additional mechanisms need independent justification rather than receiving automatic support from doctrinal familiarity.

finalArgument.thesis: This AI-generated steelman, not transcript content or wording attributable to David Enoch, argues that stance-independent normative facts vindicate action-guiding objectivity when correctly grasped ought-judgments provide reasons whose authority does not require a further independent act of allegiance.
premises: Ordinary moral judgment presents at least some reasons as answerable to features of conduct rather than to an agent's preferences, communal conventions, or contingent acceptance, creating a substantial explanatory demand for any adequate metanormative theory.

Deliberation necessarily treats some considerations as reasons bearing on what to do, and a theory that eliminates their truth-directed authority must explain how practical inquiry remains more than the organization of antecedently favored attitudes.

A justified first-person conclusion that one ought to perform an action normally ends the question of what reasons support, even though motivation may fail and unusual agents may reopen inquiry by challenging the conclusion's justification.

Higher-order demands for choosing between every standard require a reason to believe that a genuine undefeated alternative remains; the mere formal possibility of constructing privilege-star does not establish an additional practical question.

Comparative assessment should weigh breadth, centrality, and severity separately, giving foundational anomalies serious attention without automatically allowing a rare explanatory imperfection to outweigh successful treatment of pervasive deliberative practice.
finalArgument.conclusion: Robust realism therefore remains a proportionate account of normative objectivity if it explains stance-independent reasons, their indispensable deliberative role, and normal first-person closure better overall than alternatives while treating reflective anomalies as genuine but defeasible costs.

newArguments.title: The warranted-reopening distinction
newArguments.text: A residual question matters only when it is supported by a reason to doubt the operative ought-conclusion, not whenever an agent can grammatically ask what to do next. This distinguishes rational reopening from bare iterative questioning. Rival logical or normative frameworks can therefore matter when they expose an unresolved justificatory conflict, while invented privilege-star variants do not automatically create equal alternatives. Realism can acknowledge the former without accepting an endless allegiance requirement for every formally describable standard.

newArguments.title: Multi-dimensional theoretical cost
newArguments.text: Theoretical costs should be compared along distinct dimensions: how frequently a phenomenon occurs, how central it is to the practice being explained, and how severely the theory misrepresents it. A rare case may be foundational and severe, so frequency cannot settle its weight; conversely, foundational interest does not guarantee that the alleged defect is destructive. This framework lets realism assign real weight to reflective anomalies while still defending its treatment of pervasive first-person deliberation against alternatives with broader objectivity costs.

newArguments.title: Authority without motivational guarantee
newArguments.text: Action-guiding authority need not mean causal compulsion, guaranteed motivation, or immunity from renewed inquiry. A normative fact guides action when an agent who justifiably grasps it thereby has an answer to the question supported by reasons, even if weakness, distraction, or later evidence changes behavior. This interpretation preserves the distinction between settling what ought to be done and ensuring that it is done, while giving realism a clear standard against which an attitude-centered alternative must demonstrate superior explanatory coverage.

finalArgument.thesis: AI steelman: Stance-independent moral facts may secure truth beyond preference while still failing, by themselves, to determine action, because practical settlement requires a justified commitment procedure that selects among intelligible rival normative packages.
premises: If two stance-independent packages issue incompatible recommendations and an agent understands both, merely identifying which package is metaphysically privileged does not settle action unless that privilege itself supplies a practical reason for allegiance.

A nonnormative fact about privilege cannot generate practical authority without a bridge principle, while a normative bridge principle remains assessable under the same question of which normative standard an agent should follow.

A decision-centered account can close deliberation without denying truth-apt moral discourse if it distinguishes the representational content considered during reasoning from the action-committing attitude that completes reasoning.

Reflective counterexamples matter when they isolate a structural feature of guidance, but their significance should depend on diagnostic relevance and informed reproducibility rather than either population frequency or philosophical vividness alone.

Theoretical costs are heterogeneous and defeasible, so comparisons should track inferential disruption, explanatory reach, practical consequences, and repair costs instead of treating contradiction or rarity as categorically decisive.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, realism alone does not yet vindicate action-settling objectivity unless it explains how recognized normative facts rationally authorize allegiance, while a suitably developed decision-centered account remains a credible comparative alternative rather than a completed theory.

newArguments.title: Commitment-procedure asymmetry
newArguments.text: A theory can represent reasons accurately yet remain incomplete as a theory of practical settlement if it supplies no account of rational commitment. The relevant comparison is therefore not facts versus attitudes in isolation, but rival procedures for moving from represented considerations to an exclusionary commitment. Realism may contribute indispensable content while an attitude-centered procedure contributes closure. Unless realism explains that transition without presupposing the disputed package, its ontology does not uniquely perform the action-settling work claimed for it.

newArguments.title: Diagnostic invariance test
newArguments.text: A reflective anomaly deserves substantial weight when it persists under changes that remove merely verbal, sociological, and informational explanations. Test whether informed agents still face the residual question after terminology is standardized, factual ignorance is corrected, consequences are made explicit, and rival standards are represented symmetrically. Persistence across those interventions would support a structural deliberative gap; disappearance would favor the realist diagnosis of confusion or incomplete understanding. This test converts the informed-deliberator suggestion into a comparative method rather than an appeal to specialist reactions.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman for Stance-independent moral facts exist combines the side's strongest recorded claims into a measured case that directly answers the clearest objection raised in the debate.
premises: The case's strongest foundation is this recorded point: Sampson's Moorean case made a highly confident moral judgment compete directly with the more controversial premises of error theory.
A second supporting consideration is this recorded point: Enoch distinguished realism from infallibility and consensus, keeping the position responsive to disagreement and evolutionary influence.
The cumulative case also gains support from this recorded point: The sadist example clearly separated categorical moral criticism from failure relative to an agent's existing desires.

The strengthened position must directly answer this recorded limitation: Sampson's cup analogy treated rational contact with moral reality as explanatorily comparable to a well-specified physical causal relation without supplying the missing reliability mechanism.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, Stance-independent moral facts exist is supported only insofar as this combined case explains the debate's central evidence better than its rival while surviving the stated limitation.

newArguments.title: Comparative prediction test
newArguments.text: A stronger version would turn the motion into a comparison of expectations. The Stance-independent moral facts exist side should identify which observations are more likely if its account is correct, which are more likely under the rival account, and what evidence would change the conclusion. Applied to the question—Are there stance-independent moral facts that people can know and that supply genuinely categorical reasons for action?—this approach replaces isolated possibility claims with a cumulative test and prevents one attractive example from carrying the entire case.

newArguments.title: Objection stress test
newArguments.text: The case can gain credibility by adopting its opponent's strongest pressure point: Sampson's cup analogy treated rational contact with moral reality as explanatorily comparable to a well-specified physical causal relation without supplying the missing reliability mechanism. Rather than dismissing that concern, the side should state a specific repair, acknowledge what remains uncertain, and describe how an observer could distinguish its explanation from the leading alternatives. A conclusion that survives this stress test is stronger because it shows where the argument could fail and why the available evidence still favors it.

finalArgument.thesis: The AI steelman for Moral realism lacks adequate evidence combines the side's strongest recorded claims into a measured case that directly answers the clearest objection raised in the debate.
premises: The case's strongest foundation is this recorded point: Lutz's Harman-style challenge gave a parsimonious causal explanation of moral experience and demanded a distinctive evidential role for moral facts.
A second supporting consideration is this recorded point: Loeb consistently separated instrumental irrationality from moral opposition rather than covertly importing categorical reasons.
The cumulative case also gains support from this recorded point: The permissive-seemings objection forced the realists to articulate defeaters and a reliability criterion for reflective judgment.

The strengthened position must directly answer this recorded limitation: Treating causal contribution as the decisive test of evidence risked excluding abstract and rational knowledge before the comparison with mathematics, logic, and modality had been resolved.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore, Moral realism lacks adequate evidence is supported only insofar as this combined case explains the debate's central evidence better than its rival while surviving the stated limitation.

newArguments.title: Comparative prediction test
